title: A Pilgrim Before Pharaoh
summary: Jacob’s family settles in Goshen and Jacob blesses Pharaoh; Joseph carries Egypt through the famine, and the dying patriarch binds Joseph to bury him in Canaan.
historicalContext: The chapter opens in the third year of the seven-year famine, when Jacob was 130 and Joseph 39 (41:46; 45:6). Goshen lay in the eastern Nile Delta, good grazing country near the road to Canaan and apart from the farming heartland, where Egyptians held herdsmen in low regard (46:34). Egyptian records speak of royal herds kept in the Delta and of foreigners appointed to oversee them, which fits Pharaoh’s offer to the brothers. Grain was stored in the cities under royal control (41:48), and in a crisis the crown could trade it for silver, animals, land, and labour. The later Egyptian pattern in which the king owned most farmland, temples kept their own estates, and farmers paid a share of the harvest matches the arrangement this chapter describes. The name “land of Rameses” is best taken as a later label for Goshen, used so that readers would know the district.
literaryContext: Genesis 47 is a hinge between the reunion of Jacob’s family and the deathbed blessings of chapters 48–49. It moves in three scenes. Joseph presents five brothers and then his father to Pharaoh, who grants them the best of the land (vv. 1-12); Joseph manages the remaining years of famine until all Egypt’s land belongs to Pharaoh (vv. 13-26); and Jacob, seventeen years later, makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (vv. 27-31). The scenes are set in contrast: Israel receives a “possession” in Egypt while the Egyptians sell their fields; Israel is fed while Egypt hungers; Israel multiplies while Egypt’s people become Pharaoh’s servants. Jacob’s two blessings on Pharaoh frame the audience, recalling God’s promise that Abraham’s seed would bless the nations (12:3). The closing oath turns attention from Egypt’s abundance back to the land God swore to the fathers, preparing for Joseph’s own charge (50:24-25) and the exodus.
themes: The promised blessing reaching the nations
Life as a pilgrimage toward God’s promise
God’s care for his people in a strange land
Wise stewardship in a time of crisis
Faith that looks past death to the inheritance
Death as sleep with the fathers

outline.title: Pharaoh Grants the Land of Goshen
outline.summary: Joseph announces his family’s arrival and presents five brothers, who say they are shepherds and ask to sojourn in Goshen; Pharaoh gives them the best of the land and offers charge of his cattle.

outline.title: Jacob Blesses Pharaoh
outline.summary: The aged patriarch blesses Pharaoh, calls his 130 years a few and evil pilgrimage, blesses him again, and is settled with his family in Rameses, fed by Joseph.

outline.title: Joseph Brings Egypt Through the Famine
outline.summary: As the famine deepens, the people trade money, livestock, land, and finally their own service for bread and seed; Joseph makes the land Pharaoh’s and fixes a fifth of the harvest as Pharaoh’s share, exempting the priests.

outline.title: Bury Me with My Fathers
outline.summary: Israel prospers in Goshen; after seventeen years the dying Jacob makes Joseph swear to carry him out of Egypt and bury him in his fathers’ grave, and bows in worship.

verses.bibleText: Then Joseph came and told Pharaoh, and said, My father and my brethren, and their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have, are come out of the land of Canaan; and, behold, they are in the land of Goshen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph had promised his brothers that he would go up and speak to Pharaoh on their behalf (46:31), and the chapter opens with that promise kept. His report is carefully worded. He names “my father and my brethren,” then lists “their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have,” and ends with the place: “behold, they are in the land of Goshen.” Everything in the sentence presents the family as herdsmen who have come with their own means of living. They are not looking for posts at court or a share of the royal granaries.

The last clause does quiet diplomatic work. Pharaoh had already invited the family to take “the good of the land of Egypt” (45:18), and Joseph had told his father that Goshen would be their home (45:10). By reporting that they are already in Goshen, Joseph puts the place before the king without asking for it outright, leaving Pharaoh room to confirm what is already under way. The tact serves a larger purpose. Goshen kept the family together and apart, on the edge of the Delta near the road back to Canaan, where they could keep their own worship and identity instead of being absorbed into Egyptian life.

Joseph, second only to Pharaoh, does not hide his origins. He speaks of shepherds from Canaan as “my father and my brethren” in a court where such people were despised. The one who had been sold by those brothers now stands before the throne and calls them his own. The writer of Hebrews says of Christ that “he is not ashamed to call them brethren” (Hebrews 2:11).

wordNotes.term: אֶרֶץ גֹּשֶׁן (’erets Goshen) — the land of Goshen
wordNotes.explanation: Goshen was a district in the eastern Delta, suitable for grazing and close to the routes leading toward Canaan. In the Joseph story it is the place promised to the family (45:10) and requested before Pharaoh (46:34). Later it becomes the area where Israel is set apart from Egypt’s plagues (Exodus 8:22; 9:26), a sign that God distinguishes his people even while they live in a foreign land.

verses.bibleText: And he took some of his brethren, even five men, and presented them unto Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“He took some of his brethren, even five men.” The phrase behind “some of” is a Hebrew idiom meaning “from the whole number” of his brothers; Joseph chose a handful to represent the eleven. The text gives no reason for the number or the choice, and guesses about which brothers were picked go beyond what is written. Five recurs in the Joseph story (43:34; 45:22), but here it may simply describe a modest delegation.

The order of the audiences is deliberate. The brothers come first to handle the practical business of requesting land, and the aged patriarch is spared the role of a suppliant; when Jacob comes in (v. 7), he will ask for nothing and will bless. The verb “presented” means to set someone before a person of rank. Joseph had once been rushed from the dungeon to stand alone before this throne (41:14); now he introduces his family to the same king as the honoured relatives of his chief minister, standing beside them as their advocate.

wordNotes.term: וּמִקְצֵה אֶחָיו (umiqtseh ’echav) — some of his brethren
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and from the end of his brothers.” Qatseh, “end” or “extremity,” used in this way can mean the whole extent of a group, so the phrase means “from among the total number” of his brothers. A similar idiom describes Jeroboam appointing priests “of the lowest of the people,” better rendered “from among all the people” (1 Kings 12:31). It says nothing about the brothers’ rank or appearance.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto his brethren, What is your occupation? And they said unto Pharaoh, Thy servants are shepherds, both we, and also our fathers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh asks the question Joseph had predicted: “What is your occupation?” (46:33). The brothers answer exactly as they had been coached: “Thy servants are shepherds, both we, and also our fathers.” Joseph had explained the reason for this candour. Egyptians regarded keepers of sheep and goats with distaste (46:34), and an honest statement of their trade would mark the family as unsuited to court life and as people best settled at a distance from the farming population.

The answer is truthful, and that matters in a family history full of deception. Jacob had won his blessing by pretending to be Esau (27:19); the brothers had lied to their father with a bloodied coat (37:32). Joseph’s counsel avoids clever concealment and rests the family’s future on a plain statement of who they are. The phrase “both we, and also our fathers” ties them to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, all of whom lived as herdsmen moving with their flocks through the land of promise.

The occupation itself carries a long biblical resonance. Abel was “a keeper of sheep” (4:2). Moses would learn leadership in the wilderness with Jethro’s flock (Exodus 3:1), and David was taken “from the sheepfolds” to shepherd Israel (Psalm 78:70-71). The calling that Egypt despised was the one God repeatedly chose for his servants, and the LORD himself is named Israel’s Shepherd (Psalm 23:1). The brothers’ low social standing in Egypt would become a protection, guarding them from absorption into a culture that had no place for them.

wordNotes.term: רֹעֵה צֹאן (ro‘eh tso’n) — shepherds
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “shepherds of flock,” where tso’n covers sheep and goats together. The same phrase appears in Joseph’s instructions (46:32, 34), where he also notes the Egyptian aversion to such men. The participle ro‘eh, “one who pastures,” is the word used of God as the Shepherd of Israel (Psalm 80:1) and, in Jacob’s last blessing, of “the shepherd, the stone of Israel” (49:24).

verses.bibleText: They said moreover unto Pharaoh, For to sojourn in the land are we come; for thy servants have no pasture for their flocks; for the famine is sore in the land of Canaan: now therefore, we pray thee, let thy servants dwell in the land of Goshen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Having answered the question they were asked, the brothers add a request of their own. “For to sojourn in the land are we come.” They do not claim to be settlers; they present themselves as temporary residents driven by drought, “for thy servants have no pasture for their flocks; for the famine is sore in the land of Canaan.” Then comes the petition: “let thy servants dwell in the land of Goshen.”

The word “sojourn” sets the tone for the whole chapter. It is the same root Jacob will use when he calls his life a “pilgrimage” (v. 9), and it recalls the word God spoke to Abraham: “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs” (15:13). Abraham had once “sojourned” in Egypt during an earlier famine (12:10), and Isaac had been forbidden to go down there in his (26:2-3). Jacob’s family enters Egypt with God’s express permission (46:3-4), but the brothers rightly describe their stay as a temporary one. Israel would later be reminded of this every year in the confession at the harvest: “A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few” (Deuteronomy 26:5).

The brothers call themselves “thy servants” three times in two verses. Their posture is humble, and their request is modest, a place to graze. They do not mention Pharaoh’s earlier offer to give them the best of Egypt (45:18-20); they leave him free to be generous. Men who once plotted against a brother now speak with restraint and courtesy, and the request serves the purpose God had in view, a separate place where a family could grow into a nation.

wordNotes.term: לָגוּר בָּאָרֶץ (lagur ba’arets) — to sojourn in the land
wordNotes.explanation: Gur means to live as a resident alien, someone dwelling among a people without the rights of a native. The related noun ger, “stranger,” becomes a legal category in Israel’s law, which repeatedly reminds Israel that they themselves had been strangers in Egypt (Exodus 22:21; Leviticus 19:34). The brothers’ self-description anticipates the status God foretold to Abraham (15:13).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh spake unto Joseph, saying, Thy father and thy brethren are come unto thee:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh does not reply to the brothers directly. He turns to Joseph: “Thy father and thy brethren are come unto thee.” The words acknowledge the newcomers formally and place them under Joseph’s care. The Greek translation arranges verses 5-6 a little differently, with an added line reporting their arrival, but the Hebrew reads naturally as a king speaking past petitioners to his minister. Their welcome in Egypt rests on their relationship to him; they are received because they belong to the man who saved the land.

The scene illustrates a principle that runs through Scripture. Strangers find favour with the king because of one beloved son who stands at his right hand. Paul writes that God “hath made us accepted in the beloved” (Ephesians 1:6), and believers come before the King of heaven on the merits of the One who “ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Jacob’s sons brought flocks and herds, but their real security lay in the words “unto thee.”

wordNotes.term: בָּאוּ אֵלֶיךָ (ba’u ’eleykha) — are come unto thee
wordNotes.explanation: The verb bo’, “to come,” with the preposition “to you” marks Joseph as the one to whom the family has come and under whose protection they now stand. Pharaoh had used similar language when sending for them, promising “the good of all the land of Egypt is yours” (45:20). The phrase echoes Joseph’s own message to his father: “come down unto me, tarry not” (45:9).

verses.bibleText: The land of Egypt is before thee; in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell: and if thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh’s grant is generous. “The land of Egypt is before thee” echoes the words Abimelech once spoke to Abraham (20:15) and Abram’s own offer to Lot (13:9): the whole country is open for choice. Then the king specifies: “in the best of the land make thy father and brethren to dwell; in the land of Goshen let them dwell.” What the brothers had asked for modestly, Pharaoh confirms with a word of honour, calling Goshen “the best of the land.”

He adds an offer of employment. “If thou knowest any men of activity among them, then make them rulers over my cattle.” Egyptian kings kept large herds, many of them pastured in the Delta, and records mention foreign overseers placed in charge of royal livestock. The word “cattle” here refers to the larger herd animals, not only sheep. For a family of refugees this was a rare opportunity: a royal appointment with the standing and protection that came with it. Nothing further is said of the offer, and Joseph’s aim throughout was to keep his family a distinct people in Goshen, not to see them absorbed into Egypt’s service.

The verse shows how God’s blessing on Joseph overflows to his family. Earlier the Lord had blessed Potiphar’s house “for Joseph’s sake” (39:5); now Pharaoh opens his land to Joseph’s kin for the same reason. Yet the gift also carried a danger. The best of Egypt could make Canaan seem distant, and the chapter will end with Jacob insisting that Egypt is not home (vv. 29-30). Good gifts from the world must be received with open hands by those who look for a better country.

wordNotes.term: בְּמֵיטַב הָאָרֶץ (bemeitav ha’arets) — in the best of the land
wordNotes.explanation: Meitav, from the root “to be good,” means the best or choicest portion. Pharaoh uses it of Goshen here and again when Joseph settles the family (v. 11). The same word describes the restitution a man must make from the best of his own field or vineyard (Exodus 22:5) and the best of Amalek’s flocks that Saul spared against God’s command (1 Samuel 15:9).

wordNotes.term: אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל (’anshey-chayil) — men of activity
wordNotes.explanation: Chayil means strength, capability, or worth, and can refer to military valour, wealth, or competence depending on context. Here it means able and trustworthy men. Jethro advises Moses to choose “able men” of the same description as judges (Exodus 18:21), and the “virtuous woman” of Proverbs is a woman of chayil (Proverbs 31:10).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph brought in Jacob his father, and set him before Pharaoh: and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Joseph brings in his father. The verb changes: the brothers were “presented” (v. 2), but Jacob is “set before Pharaoh,” caused to stand in his presence. The meeting is no longer a matter of land and livestock. Two men face each other who represent two different orders of life. One is the ruler of the most powerful kingdom of the age, honoured by his people as a son of the gods, master of the granaries on which the whole region depends. The other is an old herdsman from Canaan, a famine refugee who owns no land, whose family has just been fed and housed by the king’s favour.

Then the narrator says, “and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.” The Hebrew verb can describe a greeting, since greetings in the ancient world were spoken as blessings, but more is happening here than courtesy. Jacob does not use the flattering forms common at court, such as “let the king live for ever” (1 Kings 1:31; Daniel 2:4). He speaks as the bearer of God’s covenant promise, invoking the favour of the LORD on a foreign king. The brothers did not bless Pharaoh; only the patriarch does, and he does so at the beginning and at the end of the audience (v. 10).

The writer of Hebrews states a principle that explains the scene: “without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better” (Hebrews 7:7). He applies it to Abraham receiving Melchizedek’s blessing, but it fits this moment as well. In every outward measure Pharaoh is the greater. In the things of God, Jacob is the greater, because he carries the promise that “in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed” (28:14). The king who had sheltered Abraham’s descendants receives a blessing in return, as God had pledged: “I will bless them that bless thee” (12:3).

The scene also shows what the promise to bless the nations looks like in practice. Jacob brings no army, wealth, or political influence to the throne room. He brings the name of God and a word of blessing, and that is a greater gift than anything Pharaoh could offer him. God’s people, however small or dependent, carry something the powerful of the world cannot provide for themselves. Paul would later urge prayer “for kings, and for all that are in authority” (1 Timothy 2:1-2), so that the blessing Jacob spoke over Pharaoh continues in the intercession of the church for those who govern.

wordNotes.term: וַיְבָרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב אֶת־פַּרְעֹה (vayevarekh Ya‘aqov ’et-Par‘oh) — and Jacob blessed Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Barak in the intensive stem means to pronounce blessing, to call down God’s favour on someone. It can be used for greetings and farewells (24:60; 2 Kings 4:29), yet in the patriarchal narratives it carries the weight of the covenant blessing passed from Abraham to Isaac to Jacob (27:27-29; 28:3-4). Melchizedek’s blessing of Abram (14:19) offers the closest parallel, a priestly benediction spoken across the lines of nation and rank.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעֲמִדֵהוּ (vaya‘amidehu) — and set him
wordNotes.explanation: A causative form of ‘amad, “to stand”: Joseph caused his father to stand before Pharaoh. The same expression is used when a person or offering is set before the LORD or before a priest for a sacred act (Leviticus 14:11; Numbers 8:13), and when Moses sets Joshua before Eleazar to be commissioned (Numbers 27:19). Here it gives Jacob’s entrance a formal, almost ceremonial weight.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Jacob, How old art thou?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh’s question is courteous and natural: “How old art thou?” The Hebrew is fuller, “How many are the days of the years of thy life?” Jacob’s great age must have been visible in his bearing, and in Egypt long life was counted a mark of divine favour. Egyptian texts held up 110 years as the ideal span of a blessed man; Joseph himself would die at that age (50:26). Jacob, at 130, had already passed it.

The question may have followed naturally from the blessing Jacob had just spoken, and it opens the way for his reply. Pharaoh asks about the length of life; Jacob will answer about its character. The king measures life in years, as rulers tended to do in a culture devoted to preserving its dead; Jacob measures it as a journey with a destination beyond itself. Scripture often treats the counting of our days as a prompt to wisdom. Moses prayed, “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psalm 90:12), and David asked to know “the measure of my days” (Psalm 39:4). Pharaoh asked out of curiosity and received more than he intended.

wordNotes.term: כַּמָּה יְמֵי שְׁנֵי חַיֶּיךָ (kammah yemey shney chayyeykha) — how old art thou
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “how many are the days of the years of your life?” The layered phrase “days of the years” is a formal idiom used in summaries of a life (25:7; 47:28). Jacob picks up the same expression three times in his reply (v. 9), turning the king’s question into a reflection on what those days have been.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said unto Pharaoh, The days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years: few and evil have the days of the years of my life been, and have not attained unto the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The days of the years of my pilgrimage are an hundred and thirty years.” Jacob changes one word in Pharaoh’s question. The king asked about the years of his “life”; Jacob answers with the years of his “pilgrimage,” his sojourning. He describes his whole existence as the stay of a temporary resident, someone dwelling in a land not his own. And he extends the description to his fathers: Abraham and Isaac also lived out “the days of their pilgrimage.”

He goes on: “few and evil have the days of the years of my life been.” The word “few” is measured against his fathers, who lived to 175 and 180 years (25:7; 35:28), and Jacob would die at 147 (v. 28). The word “evil” here means hard, troubled, painful. Flight from Esau, Laban’s exploitation, the shame of Dinah, Rachel’s death on the road, and long years of mourning for Joseph lay behind it. Much of that trouble had grown from his own deceit and favouritism, and Jacob does not dress it up before a king. His words are not a complaint against God so much as an honest confession of the cost of a life in a fallen world. Within a few years he will speak of “the God which fed me all my life long unto this day” and “the Angel which redeemed me from all evil” (48:15-16), so that the hardship and the shepherding care belong to the same life.

The New Testament takes Jacob’s word and builds on it. Hebrews says that the patriarchs “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off,” and that they “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). Jacob’s confession before Pharaoh is one of those occasions. By calling his life a sojourn, he declared that neither Canaan in its present state nor Egypt in its plenty was his final home. “They that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country,” Hebrews continues, “a better country, that is, an heavenly” (Hebrews 11:14-16).

The answer must have struck the king strangely. Before him stood a man older than any Egyptian ideal who called his long life short and treated it as a journey. Peter applies the same identity to Christians: “as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts” (1 Peter 2:11). The believer’s life, whether its days are many or few, easy or hard, is a pilgrimage toward the inheritance God has promised, and it is measured by its destination.

wordNotes.term: מְגוּרַי (megurai) — my pilgrimage
wordNotes.explanation: Magur comes from gur, “to sojourn,” the same root the brothers used in verse 4. It means the place or the period of one’s residence as an alien. God promised Abraham and Jacob “the land wherein thou art a stranger” using this word (17:8; 28:4), and Psalm 119:54 speaks of God’s statutes as songs “in the house of my pilgrimage.” The Greek version renders Jacob’s word with a term for sojourning abroad, and Hebrews draws on this vocabulary in calling the patriarchs strangers and exiles.

wordNotes.term: מְעַט וְרָעִים (me‘at vera‘im) — few and evil
wordNotes.explanation: Me‘at means little or few; ra‘im is the plural of ra‘, “bad,” here describing days that were hard and full of trouble rather than morally wicked. The same adjective describes the “evil” times that come upon people unexpectedly (Ecclesiastes 9:12). Job uses a similar pairing: “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” (Job 14:1).

verses.bibleText: And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from before Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from before Pharaoh.” The audience closes as it began, with the patriarch blessing the king. Pharaoh makes no reply to Jacob’s words about his pilgrimage, or none that the narrator records. Jacob has the last word, and it is a benediction.

The second blessing, like the first, may have been a farewell in form, but the narrative soon shows its substance. In the following verses Pharaoh grows richer than ever through Joseph’s administration, and Egypt is kept alive through the worst years of the famine (vv. 13-26). The God who had blessed Potiphar’s house for Joseph’s sake (39:5) now prospers the king who honoured Jacob’s family. The promise to Abraham worked in both directions: blessing on those who blessed his seed and, as a later Pharaoh would learn, judgment on those who oppressed it (12:3; Exodus 1:8-14).

That later contrast gives this verse its poignancy. The same phrase, going out “from Pharaoh,” will describe Moses leaving the presence of a hardened king during the plagues (Exodus 8:30; 10:6). The Pharaoh who met Jacob received blessing; a successor “which knew not Joseph” (Exodus 1:8) would choose a different path and bring ruin on his land. God’s offer of blessing to the nations was real, and Egypt’s response to Israel would shape Egypt’s own history.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּצֵא מִלִּפְנֵי פַרְעֹה (vayyetse millifney Far‘oh) — and went out from before Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Yatsa’, “to go out,” with “from before” describes leaving a superior’s presence. Joseph went out “from the presence of Pharaoh” when he was appointed over Egypt (41:46), and the same idiom describes Moses departing from Pharaoh after delivering God’s word during the plagues (Exodus 8:30; 10:6). The phrase frames Jacob’s audience as complete and dignified.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph placed his father and his brethren, and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph placed his father and his brethren, and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt.” The verb “placed” means to settle someone in a dwelling, and the noun “possession” is weighty. It is the word used of the land God promised Abraham as “an everlasting possession” (17:8) and of the burial cave Abraham bought from the Hittites (23:4, 20). In Egypt the family receives more than permission to graze; they are given property, held by a grant from the king.

The location is called “the best of the land, in the land of Rameses.” Rameses was the name of a later royal city in the eastern Delta, which Israel would one day be forced to build (Exodus 1:11), and from which they would set out in the exodus (Exodus 12:37). The name most likely reflects the district as it was known to later readers, a label for the region otherwise called Goshen (vv. 1, 4, 6), much as a modern writer might use a current place name for a town that once bore another. The verse ties the beginning of Israel’s stay in Egypt to the place where it would end.

There is an irony in the gift. Israel receives a “possession” in Egypt, while in the coming verses the Egyptians lose theirs (vv. 20, 27). Yet this possession was never meant to replace the one God had sworn to the fathers. Jacob’s instructions at the end of the chapter make that clear (vv. 29-31). God provided his people a secure home for the time of their need, so that they could grow there into a nation. Believers receive God’s present gifts with gratitude while remembering that “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

wordNotes.term: אֲחֻזָּה (’achuzzah) — a possession
wordNotes.explanation: From ’achaz, “to grasp, hold,” the noun means property held securely, often by inheritance or grant. God promised Abraham Canaan “for an everlasting possession” (17:8), and Abraham purchased Machpelah as “a possession of a buryingplace” (23:4). Jacob will use the word again in recalling God’s promise (48:4). Its use for land in Egypt highlights both God’s care and the contrast with the true inheritance.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph nourished his father, and his brethren, and all his father's household, with bread, according to their families.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph nourished his father, and his brethren, and all his father’s household, with bread.” Joseph had promised this when he revealed himself: “there will I nourish thee; for yet there are five years of famine” (45:11). Now he keeps his word. The verb means to sustain, to supply what is needed for life, and it will appear again when Joseph reassures his brothers after Jacob’s death: “I will nourish you, and your little ones” (50:21).

Behind “according to their families” stands a Hebrew phrase that reads, word for word, “to the mouth of the little ones.” The sense seems to be that provision was measured by the number in each household, down to the youngest child, so that every family received enough.

This verse serves as a bridge. It stands between the settlement of Israel and the description of Egypt’s distress, and the contrast is deliberate. While the next verse says “there was no bread in all the land,” Jacob’s household had bread, supplied freely by the son they had once sold. The brothers who had planned to let Joseph die of hunger in a pit (37:24-25) now eat at his provision. God had sent Joseph ahead “to preserve life” (45:5), and the provision for the family is the first visible proof of that purpose.

wordNotes.term: וַיְכַלְכֵּל (vaykhalkel) — and nourished
wordNotes.explanation: Kul in this intensive form means to sustain, provide for, or support. It is used of Joseph’s provision in the famine (45:11; 50:21), of God feeding Israel in the wilderness (Nehemiah 9:21), and of ravens feeding Elijah at God’s command (1 Kings 17:4). The word stresses sustained care for life, not a single gift.

verses.bibleText: And there was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very sore, so that the land of Egypt and all the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrative turns from Goshen to the rest of the land. “And there was no bread in all the land; for the famine was very sore.” The story picks up the thread left at 41:55-57, where the hungry people cried to Pharaoh and were sent to Joseph. Several years have now passed, and the crisis has deepened. The phrase “the land of Egypt and all the land of Canaan fainted” pairs the two countries, and the pairing will be repeated in the next two verses.

The verb translated “fainted” describes exhaustion to the point of collapse, a land and people worn out by want. The picture is set against the previous verse with intention. Joseph’s family had bread, while “all the land” had none.

What follows (vv. 13-26) describes how Joseph managed the remaining years of famine. The account should be read as what it is, a report of administrative measures taken in an ancient monarchy during a national emergency. It is not offered as a pattern for every economy, nor does the narrator pass judgment on it by later standards. The text’s own markers are the severity of the famine, the fact that the people lived, and their recorded response (v. 25). Later Scripture, which forbade Israel’s kings to seize land and set a lighter claim on Israel’s produce, shows that this was Egypt’s way and not the order God gave his own people.

wordNotes.term: וַתֵּלַהּ (vattelah) — and fainted
wordNotes.explanation: From lahah, a rare verb meaning to languish or be worn out; a similar-looking form in Proverbs 26:18 describes a madman, though the link between the two is uncertain. The Greek version renders the word here as “failed.” The verb portrays the whole land drained of strength, comparable to Lamentations’ picture of children fainting for hunger in the streets (Lamentations 2:19).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the corn which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the corn which they bought.” The first stage of the famine policy was simple sale. During the plentiful years a fifth of the harvest had been stored in the cities (41:34-35, 48), and now that grain was sold back to the people, with buyers from Canaan coming as Joseph’s brothers had done (42:5). The money was silver weighed out, not coined, and the verb “gathered up” is the word for gleaning: every scattered piece of silver in two countries was collected into the royal treasury.

The narrator adds a telling detail: “Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house.” With the wealth of two nations passing through his hands, Joseph did not enrich himself. The faithfulness he showed as Potiphar’s steward (39:8-9) and in the prison (39:22-23) appears again on the largest stage of his life. Jesus said, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10), and Paul required of stewards “that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). Joseph’s integrity with public resources was part of what made him fit to preserve so many lives.

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבֶר (shever) — corn
wordNotes.explanation: Shever refers to grain as provisions for sale and food, threshed grain, as distinct from seed for sowing (zera‘, v. 23). The related verb means to buy or sell grain, and it runs through the Joseph story (41:56-57; 42:1-3). Amos condemns merchants eager for the Sabbath to end so they can sell shever with false measures (Amos 8:5), showing the word’s link with the grain trade.

verses.bibleText: And when money failed in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came unto Joseph, and said, Give us bread: for why should we die in thy presence? for the money faileth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when money failed in the land of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came unto Joseph.” The silver is gone. People who still have land, animals, and households have nothing left with which to buy bread. Their plea is direct: “Give us bread: for why should we die in thy presence? for the money faileth.” From this point Canaan drops out of the account, which now concerns Joseph’s dealings with Pharaoh’s own subjects.

The words “in thy presence” express both desperation and an appeal to conscience. To let people starve before the eyes of the one who holds the granaries would be a heavy thing. The Egyptians do not accuse Joseph of greed; they present their need and look to him as the one with power to keep them alive, just as Pharaoh had told them at the start: “Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do” (41:55).

A grain market has become a matter of survival. The famine still had years to run, and giving the stores away without measure might have exhausted them before the end. The verse leaves no doubt that the people’s lives hung on what Joseph would do next.

wordNotes.term: אָפֵס כָּסֶף (’afes kasef) — money faileth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb ’afes means to come to an end, to be used up. Isaiah uses it when the extortioner comes to an end and the oppressor ceases out of the land (Isaiah 16:4). Its noun form often means “ends” or “nothingness” (Isaiah 40:17). Here the silver of two lands is simply exhausted.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said, Give your cattle; and I will give you for your cattle, if money fail.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph answers, “Give your cattle; and I will give you for your cattle, if money fail.” Silver is replaced by livestock. The arrangement had a practical side, since animals in a famine must be fed and watered when pasture has failed, and starving herds produce nothing. By taking ownership the crown took on their upkeep, and the animals probably stayed with their keepers, who tended them for the king. Joseph did not seize anything; each step is presented as an offer accepted by people who preferred it to death.

Free distribution was how Joseph cared for his father’s household (v. 12), but for a whole nation over several years he managed the stores by exchange. Readers may ask whether another course would have been kinder; the text records the decision and its result without comment. Joseph speaks here as Pharaoh’s administrator, in a different role from the weeping brother of the previous chapters (45:2). Scripture’s wisdom values the leader who plans so that the people are not left without provision (Proverbs 27:23-27), and the stores existed because Joseph had acted on God’s warning years before.

wordNotes.term: הָבוּ מִקְנֵיכֶם (havu miqneykhem) — give your cattle
wordNotes.explanation: Havu is an imperative of yahav, “to give” or “bring,” often used as a summons, “come, give.” The Egyptians themselves had used it moments before: “Give us bread” (v. 15). Miqneh, “livestock,” derives from qanah, “to acquire,” and so describes property in animals, a person’s wealth on the hoof (26:14).

verses.bibleText: And they brought their cattle unto Joseph: and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for horses, and for the flocks, and for the cattle of the herds, and for the asses: and he fed them with bread for all their cattle for that year.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they brought their cattle unto Joseph: and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for horses, and for the flocks, and for the cattle of the herds, and for the asses.” The list runs from the most valuable animals to the most ordinary. Horses come first. They were costly, prized for chariots and the display of rank, and their inclusion shows that the famine reached the wealthy as well as the poor. Horses in Egypt fit the period in which the Joseph story is set; they are mentioned earlier in connection with Joseph’s chariot (41:43) and would later pursue Israel to the sea (Exodus 14:9).

The narrator adds that Joseph “fed them with bread for all their cattle for that year.” The verb rendered “fed” is unusual. It normally means to lead or guide, especially to lead a flock gently to water and rest. The psalmist uses it when he says that God “leadeth me beside the still waters” (Psalm 23:2). Here it pictures Joseph guiding the people through that year of hunger as a shepherd leads a weak flock. The man who came from a family of shepherds becomes, in a sense, shepherd to Egypt.

The phrase “for that year” sets a time limit. The exchange of livestock carried the people through one year of the famine. The text does not say which year of the seven this was, but it seems to fall late in the period, since the following year’s request includes seed for sowing (v. 19). The people survive, though with each step they hold less of their own.

wordNotes.term: וַיְנַהֲלֵם (vaynahalem) — and he fed them
wordNotes.explanation: From nahal, “to lead with care, guide to a watering place,” used of a shepherd leading his flock gently (Isaiah 40:11) and of God guiding Israel to his holy habitation (Exodus 15:13). Psalm 23:2 uses it for the Shepherd leading beside quiet waters. Its use here suggests Joseph sustaining and guiding the people through the year, not merely selling them grain.

verses.bibleText: When that year was ended, they came unto him the second year, and said unto him, We will not hide it from my lord, how that our money is spent; my lord also hath our herds of cattle; there is not ought left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When that year was ended, they came unto him the second year,” that is, the second year after the money ran out, not the second year of the famine. The people return with a frank account of their situation: “We will not hide it from my lord, how that our money is spent; my lord also hath our herds of cattle; there is not ought left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands.”

The speech is respectful and transparent. They call Joseph “my lord” three times and conceal nothing. Silver and animals are gone; only their land and their own persons remain. The word for “bodies” is often used of a corpse, and here it conveys weakness. They come with nothing left to offer but themselves.

The irony would not have escaped the first readers. Joseph had been sold as a slave into an Egyptian household; now Egyptians come to him offering their own bodies. Yet the narrator draws no satisfaction from their plight. He lets the reader feel the famine’s complete power. Wealth, herds, and land had proved useless, and life depended on stores God had enabled Joseph to prepare. The psalmist knew that God’s eye is on those who fear him, “to keep them alive in famine” (Psalm 33:18-19).

wordNotes.term: גְּוִיָּתֵנוּ (geviyyatenu) — our bodies
wordNotes.explanation: Geviyyah means a body, frequently a dead body: Saul’s corpse fastened to the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31:10, 12), or the carcase of the lion in Judges 14:8-9. It is also used of living bodies in visions (Ezekiel 1:11; Daniel 10:6). Here it presents the Egyptians as bodies with nothing left, their persons the only property remaining.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore shall we die before thine eyes, both we and our land? buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants unto Pharaoh: and give us seed, that we may live, and not die, that the land be not desolate.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Wherefore shall we die before thine eyes, both we and our land?” The people speak of themselves and their land as sharing one fate. A field without a farmer turns to wasteland, and a farmer without seed has no future. Then they make an offer Joseph had not asked for: “buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants unto Pharaoh.” The proposal comes from the Egyptians. Joseph had asked for money and then for livestock; it is the people who offer their land and their labour.

They add a request that looks forward: “give us seed, that we may live, and not die, that the land be not desolate.” The plea for seed suggests that the end of the famine was near, or that some planting along the river was still possible. They did not want bread alone; they wanted the means to farm again.

“Servants unto Pharaoh” should be read in its ancient setting. The arrangement meant becoming tenants of the crown, bound to the land and owing a share of its produce, under a system that later Egyptian records show to have been the normal state of affairs, with most land held by the king and the temples. In a world without welfare provision, selling oneself into service was a recognized means of surviving debt or famine, and Israel’s own law later regulated such arrangements with limits and release (Leviticus 25:39-43). The text does not celebrate the loss of freedom, nor does it condemn the people for choosing life.

The phrase “that we may live, and not die” echoes Jacob’s words when he sent his sons to Egypt for grain (42:2; 43:8). The same want had driven Jacob’s household and the Egyptians to Joseph, and the same provision kept both alive. God’s purpose in sending Joseph reached beyond one family to a whole nation, as Joseph had said: “to save much people alive” (50:20).

wordNotes.term: עֲבָדִים לְפַרְעֹה (‘avadim lefar‘oh) — servants unto Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Eved can mean a slave, a servant, or a royal subject, and the range must be judged by context. Court officials were Pharaoh’s ‘avadim (41:10, 37), and the brothers had called themselves Joseph’s “servants” (44:16). Here it describes tenant farmers bound to crown land, paying a fixed share (v. 24). The same word later describes Israel’s harsh bondage in Egypt (Exodus 13:3), a reversal the chapter already anticipates.

wordNotes.term: וְהָאֲדָמָה לֹא תֵשָׁם (veha’adamah lo’ tesham) — that the land be not desolate
wordNotes.explanation: Shamem means to be desolate or deserted. ’Adamah is the cultivated ground, the soil from which man was taken and which he was set to work (2:15; 3:23). Leviticus warns that disobedience would leave Israel’s land desolate (Leviticus 26:33), and Isaiah foresees cities wasted and land “utterly desolate” (Isaiah 6:11).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh; for the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them: so the land became Pharaoh's.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh.” Joseph accepts the people’s offer, and the land changes hands field by field: “the Egyptians sold every man his field, because the famine prevailed over them.” The narrator gives the cause plainly. The sale was forced by hunger, not by trickery or violence. “So the land became Pharaoh’s.”

The outcome changed the shape of Egyptian society. Before this, much of the farmland seems to have been held by families and local landowners. In the later periods illuminated by Egyptian records, the crown and the temples held nearly all of it, and farmers worked it as tenants. The biblical account offers an explanation for how such a change could come about in a single generation of crisis.

Once again the purchase is made “for Pharaoh.” Joseph acquires nothing for himself. The narrative portrays a loyal servant who carried out his master’s interests while keeping the people alive. His loyalty to Pharaoh here parallels the faithfulness he showed to Potiphar and to the keeper of the prison, and the theme of Joseph as a trustworthy steward runs through the whole story.

The contrast with Israel is sharp. In verse 11 Joseph gave his family “a possession” in the land; here the Egyptians sell theirs. In Israel’s own law, land was never to be sold permanently, for “the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). God’s people were to hold their fields as a trust from him, and every fiftieth year the land returned to its families. Egypt’s land belonged to its king; Israel’s would belong to God.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקֶן יוֹסֵף (vayyiqen Yosef) — and Joseph bought
wordNotes.explanation: Qanah means to acquire, usually by purchase. Abraham “bought” the field of Machpelah (25:10), and Jacob bought a parcel of ground at Shechem (33:19). Boaz uses the same verb when he redeems Naomi’s land and takes Ruth as his wife (Ruth 4:9-10). Here it marks a legal transfer of land into royal ownership.

verses.bibleText: And as for the people, he removed them to cities from one end of the borders of Egypt even to the other end thereof.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And as for the people, he removed them to cities from one end of the borders of Egypt even to the other end thereof.” The Hebrew text, as it now reads, describes a movement of the population to the cities. Since the grain had been stored in the cities (41:48), gathering the people there, or in the districts around them, would have made distribution possible during the remaining months of famine. When seed was issued for planting (v. 23), the farmers would have returned to the land.

The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Greek translation read the verse differently: “he made the people servants to him from one end of Egypt to the other.” In Hebrew the two readings differ by only a couple of letters that were easily confused in copying, especially the similar-looking d and r. The alternative fits the flow of verses 19-25, where the people offer themselves as servants and later confirm the arrangement. Either reading is possible, and no doctrine turns on the choice. Both describe a sweeping change across the whole country, “from one end … to the other end.”

Whichever reading is original, the verse shows how far the famine reached. No region was spared, and the reorganisation touched every community. The account also reminds readers how quickly the security of a nation can disappear. Egypt was the granary of the ancient world, yet within a few years its people had nothing left to trade but themselves. Jesus warned against laying up treasure where it can be lost (Matthew 6:19-20) and taught his disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). The bread that kept Egypt alive had been stored by a man who trusted God’s warning, and that trust had been the land’s real security all along.

wordNotes.term: הֶעֱבִיר אֹתוֹ לֶעָרִים (he‘evir ’oto le‘arim) — he removed them to cities
wordNotes.explanation: He‘evir is a causative form of ‘avar, “to pass over,” meaning “he caused to pass” or “he moved.” The Samaritan text and the Greek version instead reflect he‘evid ’oto la‘avadim, “he made them servants.” Because the Hebrew letters for d and r look alike, the two readings could easily arise from one another. The servants reading matches the people’s offer in verse 19; the cities reading matches the storage of grain in the cities (41:48).

verses.bibleText: Only the land of the priests bought he not; for the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Only the land of the priests bought he not.” One group is exempted. The priests of Egypt received “a portion assigned them of Pharaoh,” a fixed allowance from the crown, and they lived on it. Because they did not need to buy grain, they did not need to sell their fields. The temples of Egypt were powerful institutions, holding large estates and enjoying exemption from many royal levies, and Pharaohs rarely dared to challenge them.

Joseph had personal ties to this class. He had married Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, priest of On (41:45), the great centre of sun worship. The text does not suggest that this relationship shaped his policy; it reports the exemption as an existing arrangement of Pharaoh’s, which Joseph honoured. He was a servant of the God of his fathers in a land of many gods, and he worked within the structures of the kingdom without adopting its worship.

The verse anticipates a later provision in Israel. The Levites and priests of Israel received no tribal inheritance of land, for “the LORD is their inheritance” (Deuteronomy 18:1-2), and they lived on the tithes and offerings of the people (Numbers 18:21). The parallel is not exact: Egypt’s priests kept their land, while Israel’s priests had none. Yet both systems recognized that those set apart for religious service should be supported by the community. Paul applies the principle to the ministers of the gospel: “they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar” (1 Corinthians 9:13-14).

wordNotes.term: חֹק (choq) — a portion
wordNotes.explanation: Choq, from a root meaning “to engrave” or “inscribe,” usually means a statute, but it can also mean a fixed allotment or prescribed share, as of food (Proverbs 30:8, “food convenient for me,” literally “my portion of bread”) or of work. It appears again in verse 26, where Joseph makes the fifth part “a law” (choq). The priests’ portion was a set allowance guaranteed by royal decree.

verses.bibleText: Then Joseph said unto the people, Behold, I have bought you this day and your land for Pharaoh: lo, here is seed for you, and ye shall sow the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph now addresses the people formally: “Behold, I have bought you this day and your land for Pharaoh.” The words state the legal outcome, much as a witness might confirm a transaction at the city gate (compare Ruth 4:9). He does not leave them there. Immediately he adds, “lo, here is seed for you, and ye shall sow the land.”

The gift of seed is the turning point of the whole account. Bread kept the people alive from one season to the next; seed restored their future. With it they could return to the fields, plant, and harvest again. The people had asked for seed “that we may live, and not die” (v. 19), and Joseph grants their request.

The arrangement echoes a basic pattern of creation. God gave Adam the ground to till and seed-bearing plants for food (1:29; 2:15), and after the flood he promised that “seedtime and harvest … shall not cease” (8:22). In a world where that rhythm had broken down for seven years, Joseph’s distribution of seed is a step back toward the order God had promised to sustain. Paul speaks of God as the One who “ministereth seed to the sower” and “bread for your food” (2 Corinthians 9:10).

wordNotes.term: הֵא־לָכֶם זֶרַע (he’-lakhem zera‘) — lo, here is seed for you
wordNotes.explanation: He’ is a rare interjection, “here, behold,” found also in Ezekiel 16:43 and Daniel 2:43 (Aramaic). Zera‘ means seed for sowing and also offspring, the word used for the promised “seed” of the woman and of Abraham (3:15; 22:17-18). In this verse its sense is agricultural: grain to plant so that the land may again bear a harvest.

verses.bibleText: And it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The terms of the new arrangement follow: “it shall come to pass in the increase, that ye shall give the fifth part unto Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own.” The people would farm the land as tenants of the crown, paying a fifth of their harvest and keeping the rest. The four parts were for “seed of the field, and for your food, and for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.”

The fifth part was already familiar. During the seven years of plenty Joseph had collected a fifth of the produce to store against the famine (41:34). That had been an emergency measure in years of abundance; now it became the permanent rate on land owned by the crown. By the standards of the ancient world, a fifth was moderate. Agreements elsewhere in the region commonly claimed a third of the crop or more in exchange for land and seed, so the people were left with a substantial share of their harvest.

The list of what the four parts would cover shows concern for ordinary life: the next year’s planting, the family’s table, the household, and the little ones. Joseph’s provision for Egyptian children mirrors his care for his own clan (v. 12).

Israel would know a different law. God claimed a tenth of the land’s increase as holy to himself (Leviticus 27:30), not as rent to a king but as an acknowledgment that the land and its produce came from him. Samuel warned that an Israelite king would take a tenth of their grain and flocks (1 Samuel 8:15, 17), and the people of God were meant to remember that no human ruler held the land as God did.

wordNotes.term: הַחֲמִישִׁית (hachamishit) — the fifth part
wordNotes.explanation: From chamesh, “five,” the word means one fifth. Joseph first proposed taking a fifth of the land’s produce during the years of plenty (41:34). In Israel’s law the fifth appears as the added payment for restitution of holy things or wrongs against a neighbour (Leviticus 5:16; 6:5), a different use of the same fraction.

verses.bibleText: And they said, Thou hast saved our lives: let us find grace in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh's servants.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The people’s answer is the narrator’s chief evidence for how the arrangement was received. “Thou hast saved our lives: let us find grace in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants.” They do not speak of injustice or loss. They speak of rescue.

Modern readers sometimes judge Joseph harshly, seeing in this chapter the creation of a servile peasantry and the concentration of wealth in a king’s hands. Others praise him as a model economist. Both responses read the passage from a distance the text does not invite. The narrative is set in an ancient monarchy where the king was regarded as the owner of the land and service to the crown was the common condition of farmers. It records a crisis in which the alternative to Joseph’s measures was mass starvation. The narrator does not hold up the policy as God’s ideal for society, and later Scripture shows that God wanted something different for Israel. Nor does he condemn it; he reports the gratitude of those who lived through it.

The words “thou hast saved our lives” stand at the centre of Joseph’s whole story. His brothers had meant to take his life (37:20), yet God used him to keep a family and a nation alive. Joseph would later sum it up: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive” (50:20).

The verse also points beyond Joseph. The Egyptians offered themselves as servants to the one who saved their lives. The New Testament calls believers to a similar response toward Christ, who gave his life for them: “ye are not your own … ye are bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Joseph saved bodies through a famine; Christ redeems the whole person for eternal life, and service to him is freedom, for his yoke is easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30).

wordNotes.term: הֶחֱיִתָנוּ (hecheyitanu) — thou hast saved our lives
wordNotes.explanation: A causative form of chayah, “to live,” meaning “you have kept us alive.” Joseph used the same verb when he told his brothers that God sent him “to save your lives by a great deliverance” (45:7) and again when he spoke of saving “much people alive” (50:20). The Egyptians unknowingly echo the theological heart of the Joseph story.

wordNotes.term: נִמְצָא־חֵן בְּעֵינֵי אֲדֹנִי (nimtsa’-chen be‘eyney ’adoni) — let us find grace in the sight of my lord
wordNotes.explanation: To “find grace (chen) in someone’s eyes” is to receive their favour, a phrase used throughout Genesis by those seeking kindness from a superior (32:5; 33:8). Noah “found grace in the eyes of the LORD” (6:8). Jacob will use the same words to Joseph in verse 29, so the expression links the Egyptians’ request with the patriarch’s.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth part; except the land of the priests only, which became not Pharaoh's.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth part.” The arrangement became a permanent statute. The narrator adds the familiar note “unto this day,” which he uses to connect events with conditions known to his readers (compare 32:32; 35:20). The writer was familiar with Egypt’s land laws, which fits Moses’ upbringing at the Egyptian court (Acts 7:22).

The exception is repeated: “except the land of the priests only, which became not Pharaoh’s.” Egyptian practice over many centuries matches this picture, with the crown and the temples holding the land and farmers paying a share of their produce.

The verse closes the account of Joseph’s administration. Pharaoh emerges from the famine immensely enriched, owning the land, the livestock, the silver, and the service of the people. In this the blessing Jacob pronounced on Pharaoh (vv. 7, 10) found visible expression. The king who had welcomed Abraham’s seed prospered through the son of Jacob. The narrator, however, does not end the chapter in Pharaoh’s court. He turns at once to Goshen, where Israel was gaining possessions (v. 27), and then to Jacob’s deathbed. Egypt’s wealth is reported; Israel’s hope is the subject.

The statute also became part of the background against which Israel would later understand its own calling. Moses’ first readers knew Egypt as the house of bondage, where land and people belonged to a king. God’s law for Israel gave each family its own inheritance in the land, protected by the jubilee, and claimed only the tithe as holy to the LORD. The comparison invites gratitude: the God who redeemed Israel was a far gentler Master than any Pharaoh, and the obedience he asked rested on deliverance already given (Exodus 20:2).

wordNotes.term: לְחֹק עַד־הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה (lechoq ‘ad-hayyom hazzeh) — a law unto this day
wordNotes.explanation: Choq here means a fixed statute, as in Israel’s “statutes” given by God (26:5; Exodus 15:25). The phrase “unto this day” appears often in Genesis to tie a past event to a custom or place still known to the readers (19:37-38; 32:32). David’s ruling that the spoil be shared with those who stayed by the baggage is likewise called “a statute and an ordinance for Israel unto this day” (1 Samuel 30:25).

verses.bibleText: And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the country of Goshen; and they had possessions therein, and grew, and multiplied exceedingly.” The narrator returns to the family after the long account of Egypt’s distress, and the contrast is plain. While the Egyptians sold their fields to survive, Israel acquired property. While Egypt’s people became Pharaoh’s servants, Israel grew and flourished.

The name “Israel” here stands for the whole family, and the grammar shows it: the verb “dwelt” is singular, the following verbs are plural. The patriarch and the people descended from him are treated as one. The word “dwelt” suggests settled residence. Jacob had once “dwelt in the land wherein his father was a stranger” (37:1); now his house dwells in Egypt, still strangers there, yet secure.

The words “grew, and multiplied” recall God’s first blessing on humanity, “Be fruitful, and multiply” (1:28), renewed to Noah (9:1) and promised to Jacob himself at Bethel: “be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee” (35:11). At Beersheba, on the way down, God had said, “I will there make of thee a great nation” (46:3). Within a single verse, the narrator shows that promise beginning to be kept. The book of Exodus opens with the same words, in fuller form: “the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty” (Exodus 1:7).

The verse carries a quiet warning as well. Prosperity in Egypt was a gift, but it could become a trap. Comfortable possessions in a foreign land could make the promised land seem unnecessary. The rest of the chapter answers that danger. Jacob, though he had property in Goshen, would not let his family forget where their true inheritance lay.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּאָחֲזוּ בָהּ (vayye’achazu vah) — and they had possessions therein
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of ’achaz, “to grasp,” meaning “they acquired holdings” or “they took possession.” It shares its root with ’achuzzah, “possession,” in verse 11. The same verb describes the Israelites settling and acquiring property in Canaan in later times (Joshua 22:9, 19) and Shechem’s invitation to Jacob’s family to “get you possessions” in their land (34:10).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְרוּ וַיִּרְבּוּ מְאֹד (vayyifru vayyirbu me’od) — and grew, and multiplied exceedingly
wordNotes.explanation: Parah, “to be fruitful,” and rabah, “to multiply,” form the pairing of the creation blessing (1:28) and its renewal to Noah (9:1, 7) and Jacob (35:11). Their combination here marks the fulfilment of that blessing in Israel. Exodus 1:7 repeats and intensifies the pair at the start of the next book.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years: so the whole age of Jacob was an hundred forty and seven years.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years: so the whole age of Jacob was an hundred forty and seven years.” The narrator moves forward seventeen years in a sentence.

The number seventeen forms a symmetry with the beginning of the Joseph story. Joseph was seventeen years old when his father sent him to his brothers and he disappeared (37:2). For seventeen years Jacob had cared for his son in Canaan; now for seventeen years the son cared for his father in Egypt. The loss and the restoration are balanced, as though God gave back to Jacob the years that grief had taken.

Jacob’s age at death, 147 years, falls short of Abraham’s 175 (25:7) and Isaac’s 180 (35:28), as Jacob had said before Pharaoh: “they have not attained unto the days of the years of the life of my fathers” (v. 9). Yet he lived far beyond the Egyptian ideal of 110, and beyond Joseph (50:26) and Moses (Deuteronomy 34:7). His “few” days were many by any measure after him.

The formula “the whole age” or “the days of the years of his life” usually comes at a patriarch’s death notice (25:7; 35:28). Here it appears early, several chapters before Jacob actually breathes his last (49:33). The narrator gives the total in advance and then lingers over the final scenes: the oath about burial, the blessing of Joseph’s sons, and the prophetic words to all twelve sons. Jacob’s last days receive more space than those of any other patriarch, because through them God’s promises would be passed to the tribes of Israel.

wordNotes.term: וַיְחִי יַעֲקֹב (vay’chi Ya‘aqov) — and Jacob lived
wordNotes.explanation: Chayah, “to live,” in the simple narrative form. The same opening, “and he lived,” punctuates the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11, which measure each life in years. Its use here recalls those records and places Jacob in the line of patriarchs whose lives are counted (5:3; 11:26). The Greek version uses a verb meaning “lived on,” stressing the years Jacob survived in Egypt after he thought his life was ending.

verses.bibleText: And the time drew nigh that Israel must die: and he called his son Joseph, and said unto him, If now I have found grace in thy sight, put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh, and deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the time drew nigh that Israel must die.” The narrator uses Jacob’s covenant name, Israel, as the patriarch prepares for death. The phrase “the time drew nigh” is used again of David as his death approached and he charged Solomon (1 Kings 2:1). Both men use their last strength to secure the future of God’s purpose.

Jacob calls Joseph, not all his sons. Joseph held the power in Egypt to carry out his father’s wishes, and Pharaoh’s permission would be needed to take a body out of the country (50:4-6). Jacob addresses his son with a phrase normally used toward a superior: “If now I have found grace in thy sight.” The old patriarch speaks as a suppliant to the vizier, recognizing Joseph’s position, though the request comes from a father to a son.

He asks for an oath in the ancient form: “put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh.” Abraham had required the same of his servant when sending him to find a wife for Isaac from his own kindred (24:2, 9). In both cases the oath concerned the future of the covenant family and their relation to the land of promise. The gesture, placing the hand near the source of life and descendants, bound the one swearing to the patriarch’s posterity and to the God who had made promises to it.

The content of the oath is “deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt.” The pairing “kindly and truly” describes loyal love that can be relied on. Kindness cannot be forced, and so faithfulness is joined to it, making the promise sure. Jacob asks Joseph to show this loyalty to him after he is dead, when he can no longer see or enforce it. Ruth was praised for kindness of this kind shown to the dead (Ruth 1:8; 2:20).

“Bury me not … in Egypt” is the heart of the request. Egypt offered Jacob every comfort, and Egyptian burial would have been elaborate and honourable. But to be buried there would be to accept Egypt as home. Jacob would not let even his body belong to the land of his sojourning. His request was an act of faith in God’s word: the promise that Canaan would belong to his descendants (28:13; 35:12) and God’s pledge at Beersheba, “I will also surely bring thee up again” (46:4).

wordNotes.term: חֶסֶד וֶאֱמֶת (chesed ve’emet) — kindly and truly
wordNotes.explanation: Chesed is loyal, covenant love, kindness that goes beyond obligation; ’emet is faithfulness, reliability, truth. Together they describe steadfast loyalty. Abraham’s servant praised God for not withholding his “mercy and truth” (24:27), Jacob confessed himself unworthy of God’s “mercies” and “truth” (32:10), and God proclaimed himself “abundant in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6). Jacob asks Joseph to reflect that divine quality toward him.

wordNotes.term: שִׂים־נָא יָדְךָ תַּחַת יְרֵכִי (sim-na’ yadkha tachat yerekhi) — put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh
wordNotes.explanation: Yarekh, “thigh,” can stand by euphemism for the loins, the seat of procreation, so that descendants are said to come out of a man’s thigh (46:26; Exodus 1:5, “loins”). The gesture appears only here and in Abraham’s charge to his servant (24:2, 9). In both scenes the oath protects the covenant line and its tie to the promised land.

verses.bibleText: But I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their buryingplace. And he said, I will do as thou hast said.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their buryingplace.” Jacob describes his death as lying down with his fathers. The Hebrew verb is the ordinary word for lying down to sleep, and this expression for death runs through the Old Testament. Scripture speaks of death this way because death, for God’s people, is a rest from which they will be awakened. Daniel foresees that “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake” (Daniel 12:2), and Jesus used the same language of a dead girl and of his friend Lazarus: “Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep” (John 11:11).

The phrase does not imply that Jacob expected to join his fathers in a conscious existence elsewhere. He speaks of lying with them in their burial place, the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah were already buried (49:29-31). The dead, in Scripture’s view, do not live on as disembodied spirits; they rest in the grave, unconscious, until God calls them. “The dead know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5), and Peter could say on the day of Pentecost that David “is not ascended into the heavens” (Acts 2:29, 34). Jacob’s hope looked forward to the resurrection, when the Lord would raise the sleepers and give them the inheritance he had promised.

That is why the burial place mattered: the request rested on the promise. God had pledged the land to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob personally, “to thee will I give it, and to thy seed” (28:13), yet none of them had received it. Hebrews notes that all of them died still waiting (Hebrews 11:13). The only way such a promise could be kept to them was by resurrection. By choosing to rest in Canaan, Jacob laid claim to the land beforehand and declared that he expected to rise in it.

Joseph replies simply, “I will do as thou hast said.” He would later make his own brothers swear to carry his bones out of Egypt (50:25), and Moses would fulfil that oath at the exodus (Exodus 13:19). The family’s hope ran from generation to generation, each looking past death to God’s faithfulness.

The New Testament gathers all of this into the promise of Christ’s return. “The Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout … and the dead in Christ shall rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). On that day the patriarchs will receive the inheritance for which they waited, and with them all who have fallen asleep trusting the same promise (Hebrews 11:39-40).

wordNotes.term: וְשָׁכַבְתִּי עִם־אֲבֹתַי (veshakhavti ‘im-’avotai) — but I will lie with my fathers
wordNotes.explanation: Shakhav means to lie down, especially to sleep. With “with his fathers” it becomes a standard expression for death, used of Moses (Deuteronomy 31:16), David (1 Kings 2:10), and many kings. Job uses the verb when he says, “so man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake” (Job 14:12), linking lying down in death with a future awakening. The Greek version renders it with the word for sleeping.

wordNotes.term: בִּקְבֻרָתָם (biqvuratam) — in their buryingplace
wordNotes.explanation: Qevurah means a grave or burial site. Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah as “a possession of a buryingplace” (23:4, 9, 20), the only land in Canaan the patriarchs ever owned. Jacob later lists all who rest there (49:29-31), and his sons carry out his wish (50:13). Jacob’s insistence on that grave ties his death to the land God promised.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Swear unto me. And he sware unto him. And Israel bowed himself upon the bed's head.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, Swear unto me. And he sware unto him.” Joseph’s promise was not enough for Jacob; he wanted an oath. Jacob did not doubt his son’s sincerity, but an oath placed the promise before God and made it binding beyond Joseph’s goodwill. It also gave Joseph something to present to Pharaoh, who might otherwise have hesitated to let his chief minister leave the country to bury a foreigner. When the time came, Joseph would tell Pharaoh, “My father made me swear,” and Pharaoh would answer, “Go up, and bury thy father, according as he made thee swear” (50:5-6).

“And Israel bowed himself upon the bed’s head.” Having secured the oath, Jacob worships. The verb means to bow down in reverence, the posture of worship before God. His gratitude is directed to the God whose promise he trusted and whose faithfulness he had known through a life of trouble.

The Hebrew consonants of the word translated “bed” can be read in two ways. With one set of vowels it means “bed” (mittah); with another, “staff” (matteh). The vowel points were added to the Hebrew text centuries after it was written, and the earlier Greek translation reads “staff”: Israel bowed “upon the top of his staff.” The writer of Hebrews follows the Greek reading: “By faith Jacob, when he was a dying, blessed both the sons of Joseph; and worshipped, leaning upon the top of his staff” (Hebrews 11:21). Either picture suits an aged man near death, too weak to prostrate himself fully, bowing as he could. The staff reading has a particular fitness. Jacob had crossed the Jordan with only his staff (32:10); now, at the end of his pilgrimage, he leans on a staff to worship the God who had brought him through.

Hebrews places this act among the great deeds of faith. It was faith because Jacob worshipped over a promise he would not live to see fulfilled. He had secured a grave in Canaan, not a throne, yet he bowed in thanksgiving as though the inheritance were already his. Faith, Hebrews says, is “the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). The patriarch who began life grasping at his brother’s heel ends it bowing in worship, and that transformation is the work of God’s grace through the long years of his pilgrimage.

wordNotes.term: עַל־רֹאשׁ הַמִּטָּה (‘al-ro’sh hammittah) — upon the bed’s head
wordNotes.explanation: The consonants mth may be read mittah, “bed,” as in the traditional Hebrew vowels, or matteh, “staff,” as the Greek version and Hebrews 11:21 read it. Mittah appears in 48:2 and 49:33, where Jacob sits up and later gathers his feet into his bed. Matteh is Judah’s staff given as a pledge (38:18). Both readings picture an old man worshipping as his strength allowed; David likewise “bowed himself upon the bed” in thanksgiving near the end of his life (1 Kings 1:47).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ (vayyishtachu) — and bowed himself
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to bow down or prostrate oneself, either before a human superior (33:3; 42:6) or, as most often, before God in worship (22:5; 24:26). Here it marks Jacob’s response of worship once his burial is assured. The scene may recall Joseph’s dream that his father would bow before him (37:10), yet the context points to worship offered to God.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: If someone asked you to sum up your life so far in one sentence, what would you say, and where would you say you are headed?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: Living as a guest in Egypt and dependent on Pharaoh’s favour, Jacob blesses the king in God’s name, confesses that his life is a pilgrimage, and with his last strength binds his son to carry his body back to the land God promised, showing a faith that rests on God’s word beyond death.
discussionQuestions: Why is it striking that Jacob, a famine refugee, blesses Pharaoh, and what does Hebrews 7:7 suggest about the meaning of that act?
What did Jacob mean by calling his 130 years a “pilgrimage,” and how does Hebrews 11:13-16 develop that word?
How should we read Joseph’s famine policy in its ancient setting, and what do the Egyptians’ own words in verse 25 add?
What contrasts does the chapter draw between Israel in Goshen and the people of Egypt?
Why was it so important to Jacob to be buried in Canaan rather than in Egypt, and what does his request reveal about his hope?
commonMisunderstandings: Jacob’s blessing was more than a polite greeting to a king; the bearer of God’s promise pronounced God’s favour on a ruler who had shown kindness to his people.

The chapter does not offer Joseph’s land policy as a model economic system for all times, nor does it present it as tyranny; it reports a crisis measure the people themselves accepted as their rescue.
Jacob’s wish to lie with his fathers does not mean he expected to join their conscious spirits; Scripture calls death a sleep, and his hope looked to the land and the resurrection God would bring.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the pilgrim theme central. Jacob stands before the most powerful man in the world as a stranger and sojourner, yet he is the one who blesses, and he ends the chapter refusing to let Egypt claim even his bones. Faith treats every earthly dwelling as temporary and rests its future on God’s promise.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Your days, like Jacob’s, may feel few and hard, but they are a pilgrimage with a destination; place your hope where he placed his, in the God who keeps his promises past the grave and will raise his sleeping people to their inheritance.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The believer’s hope beyond death: life is a pilgrimage, death is a sleep, and God’s people look forward to the resurrection and the promised inheritance at Christ’s coming.
flow: Before Pharaoh, Jacob called his whole life a pilgrimage, short and full of trouble.
Hebrews explains that the patriarchs confessed themselves strangers because they sought a better, heavenly country.
Jacob asked to “lie with” his fathers in Canaan, using Scripture’s language of death as sleep.
God’s promise of the land could not be fulfilled for Jacob in his lifetime; it awaits the resurrection, when Christ returns and raises the dead.
Every person can join the pilgrims by trusting the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who is not the God of the dead but of the living.
simpleIllustrations: A traveller living out of a suitcase in a hotel may enjoy the room, but he never hangs pictures on the walls; his home is elsewhere, and everything about the way he lives shows it.
Jacob’s instructions for his burial were like a man leaving a forwarding address: he would not stay in Egypt, and he wanted everyone to know where to find him on the morning of the resurrection.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you, like Jacob, confess that you are a pilgrim here and place your hope in the God who will raise his people and bring them home?
cautions: Do not turn Jacob’s “few and evil” days into an argument that the life of faith is joyless; his later blessings show deep gratitude for God’s shepherding care.
Avoid both praising and condemning Joseph’s famine policy by modern standards; let the text’s own setting and the people’s response shape the discussion.
Present death as sleep from the text gently, with comfort for the bereaved, without polemic.

reflectionQuestions: Do I live as a pilgrim, or have I settled so comfortably in my Egypt that I have forgotten the promised land?
Am I a channel of God’s blessing to the people in authority over me, even when I depend on them?
How would I describe the days of my life if someone in power asked me, and would my answer point to God?
Do I manage what has been entrusted to me with the wisdom and fairness that preserve the lives of others?
Have I settled where I want my hope to rest when I fall asleep in death?
